title: Field-induced first order transitions and phase coexistence in the Kitaev quantum spin liquid candidate BaCo2(AsO4)2
authors: Tanner J. Legvold, Bin Gao, Rong-Zhu Lin, Violet Williams, Tong Chen, Dehong Yu, Chien-Lung Huang, Gage Eichman, Renjie Lui, Benedetta Flebus, Pengcheng Dai, Douglas Natelson
abstract: BaCo2(AsO4)2 (BCAO) is an insulating Kitaev quantum spin liquid candidate with a rich low-temperature phase diagram. Below 5 K, it exhibits double-zigzag magnetic order. Upon application of an in-plane magnetic field, the magnetic structure first transforms into an up-up-down (UUD) state near 0.12 T and then enters a fully spin-polarized ferromagnetic (FM) state near 0.5 T. In the narrow field regime close to the polarized phase, a finite residual thermal conductivity has been reported, suggesting a possible field-induced quantum spin liquid phase. Using neutron scattering, we show that the field-induced double-zigzag-to-UUD transition near 0.15 T is accompanied by the emergence of a cluster of localized UUD spin excitations that coexist with conventional spin waves. Upon further increasing field, BCAO undergoes a first-order UUD-to-FM transition with coexistence of UUD and FM phases, accompanied by a sharp response in the spin Seebeck coefficient. These results do not support a quantum spin liquid scenario near the UUD-to-FM critical field. Instead, modeling indicates that the broad excitations arise from bound spin-flip pairs, while a low-lying dispersive branch near the FM phase boundary carries the same sign of magnetization as the FM order. These excitations naturally account for the observed sign of the spin Seebeck response and are likely relevant to the thermal conductivity near the critical field.
summary: This study experimentally investigates field-induced transitions in the Kitaev candidate BaCo2(AsO4)2. Using neutron scattering and spin transport measurements, the authors find evidence for first-order phase coexistence rather than a continuous quantum liquid evolution. They conclude that observed excitations are better explained by bound magnon pairs, challenging previous interpretations of anomalous thermal transport.
main_problem: The study investigates field-induced first-order magnetic transitions and phase coexistence within BaCo2(AsO4)2, a material proposed as a Kitaev quantum spin liquid candidate.
main_result: Neutron scattering and transport measurements reveal that the transitions are first-order, characterized by phase coexistence (UUD/FM), rather than continuous evolution toward a QSL state. Theoretical modeling suggests observed excitations arise from bound spin-flip pairs.
method: The research combines inelastic neutron scattering to probe magnetic excitations with transport measurements like the Spin Seebeck effect and theoretical modeling of magnon interactions.
model_or_system: The system is BaCo2(AsO4)2, an insulating material with Co2+ ions arranged on a honeycomb lattice. It exhibits multiple magnetic phases (double-zigzag, UUD, FM) whose transitions are studied under applied magnetic fields.
key_observables: Magnetic order parameters (UUD, FM), excitation spectra (spin waves, localized modes), thermal conductivity ($\kappa/T$), and the sign/magnitude of the Spin Seebeck coefficient.
important_parameters: Applied in-plane magnetic field ($B$) near critical fields like 0.15 T and 0.5 T; temperature ($T$); energy scales (meV).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that observed excitations can be modeled by bound spin-flip pairs rather than requiring a gapless spinon Fermi surface characteristic of a true QSL.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnetic phase diagram, field-dependent excitation spectra showing mode separation and collapse at transitions, and transport measurements (SMR/SSE) confirming hysteresis associated with first-order changes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the complex magnetic phase diagram via neutron scattering to detailing evidence of first-order transitions through multiple probes (INS, SMR, SSE), culminating in theoretical modeling that reinterprets anomalous transport signals as bound excitations rather than QSL signatures.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant because it uses advanced spectroscopic and transport techniques to test the boundaries between exotic quantum states (QSLs) and conventional magnetically ordered phases, providing crucial insights into strongly correlated magnetic materials dynamics.
